title: The logical upshot (Ultimately / Then / In the end)
subtitle: Transitions · 13 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **13 of the official questions in Transitions are this one** — 1 Easy, 0 Medium, 12 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- This is usually the hardest tier.
- The passage is abstract and dense, often about literature or the history of ideas.
- The blank may sit mid-sentence, e.g. 'It may not have been..., ______, that...'.
- Sentence two is a summary judgment or an inference drawn from the setup, not a single effect.
- Choices are several words that all sound plausible for adding or concluding: to that end, moreover, hence, then, ultimately.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Decide whether sentence two is a final judgment that brings together tensions described earlier ('ultimately', 'in the end') or a reasonable inference that follows from the premise ('then', in the sense of 'it follows that').
- 2) Test each decoy strictly: 'to that end' needs a stated goal, 'hence' needs a direct cause, and 'moreover' needs a separate new point.
- 3) Keep the choice whose precise requirement the passage actually meets.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: The decoys are near-synonyms, and each has a narrow condition you forget to check. 'To that end' introduces how a purpose is carried out, not a conclusion. 'Hence' needs a mechanical cause-effect link. 'Moreover' adds a new point.
You pick whichever one 'sounds academic' instead of testing its exact logical job.

sections.heading: You are losing these
